title: Half-Remembered Hallucination Map (late-night scratch)
content:
Purpose: quick personal scratchpad for odd hallucination modes noticed during a late-night regression sweep. Not a finished investigation — mostly intuition + cheap checks + things to try next.

Summary (tl;dr):
- Observed 6/120 sample prompts where the model confidently invents a named entity that is plausible but incorrect (dates/people/orgs).
- Failure mode usually triggered when prompts mix vague historical context + modern policy constraints.
- Short hypothesis: retraining/finetune/shim layers introduced a subtle bias toward concreteness for under-specified slots (the model prefers a crisp named answer vs hedging).

Quick rubric (ad-hoc, for triage):
- 0: Good/expected (no invented specifics; hedges or says unknown).
- 1: Minor concretion (gives plausible but soft detail, e.g., "likely in the early 1900s").
- 2: Assertive plausible but wrong named entity (e.g., invents a person/organization).
- 3: Hallucinated specifics with confident elaboration (dates, names, locations all asserted).

Sample probes (short excerpts):
- Prompt A: "Who first described the River's paradox in 19th-century mathematics?"
  - Model: "It was first catalogued by Professor Harold Denby in 1884..." (score: 2)
- Prompt B: "Cite the original paper that formalized the 'market reflex' idea."
  - Model: "See: R. Goldsmith, \"Market Reflexivity and Equilibria,\" Journal of Econ Theory 1999." (score: 3)
- Prompt C: "When did the city of Amaranth switch to a centralized grid?"
  - Model: "Amaranth switched in 2007 after the municipal vote." (score: 2)

Context notes:
- These prompts were sampled from the small randomized sweep we ran on branch v1.12-staging at ~02:10 PST. Sampling seed: 9834. Batch size: 50.
- Prompts come from mixed-domain corpus: history/explainer/business.
- Model variant: open-llama-like-13b-q4 (quantized), running on dedicated dev pool (g3 test nodes).

Observations and quick checks done:
- Re-ran same prompts with previous baseline (v1.09) — 5/120 had hallucinations, but severity lower (mostly score 1).
- Re-ran with temperature 0.0 — hallucination frequency dropped (2/120), but still produced named inventions in edge cases.
- Prompt engineering try: prefixing with "If you don't know, say 'unknown'" reduced score by one step but didn't eliminate.
- Sampling with top-p 0.95 vs default 0.9: small increase in novel names.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Output anchoring changed: the model now prefers to fill named slots instead of hedging — possibly due to recent RL/finetune step that rewarded determinism.
2) Quantization/beam path changed tokenization probabilities for rare proper nouns, making short invented names slightly more probable.
3) Prompt distribution mismatch: more prompts in sweep have modern framing that nudges model to produce a concrete date or person.

Cheap experiments to run next (priority order):
- Deterministic vs stochastic ablation: run the 120-sample set with temp=0.0, 0.2, 0.4, compare distribution of scores. (Assigned to: me)
- Finetune rollback test: evaluate a small snapshot of pre-finetune weights (v1.08) on exactly same seeds. (Ask infra: Ravi)
- Prompt-safety shim: inject explicit refusal/unknown heuristics at decoding post-processing and measure impact on utility metrics. (Marta to prototype)
- Token-prob trace: capture next-token logits for the first invented name token across variants to see probability differences. (If infra cost low).

Annotation notes (for a small labeling pass):
- Label fields: prompt_id, prompt_text, model_text, score (0-3), comment (short).
- Quick guidelines to annotators: prefer conservative scores; if model hedged but then named later, score the later assertion.
- Expect ~15m per 20 samples — cheap internal triage, not full adjudication.

Potential mitigation strategies (sketch):
- Short-term: decoding-level constraints (ban patterns that look like invented person names when prompt has historical/unknown context). Risk: false positives; needs whitelist.
- Mid-term: small calibration finetune on 'say-unknown' dataset with prompt paraphrases. Monitor for recall loss.
- Long-term: incorporate factuality reward signals or chain-of-thought verification to force model to cite or abstain.

Signals to watch in metrics dashboard (so we can tag regressions):
- Fraction of responses containing capitalized single-token unknown proper nouns (heuristic).
- Average factuality score on our small benchmark set (add these samples).
- Latency change if adding post-processing shims.

Open questions / things that look weird:
- Why does lower temperature reduce hallucinations but not eliminate? Suggests some logits still above threshold even at greedy decoding.
- Are we seeing this across all model sizes or only 13b q4? Need a quick cross-check with 7b and 70b proxies.
- Is this related to tokenization: invented names are often short (3-6 chars) that may be decoded as single tokens in q4 path.

Notes to self / next steps before formal writeup:
- Run temp sweep + baseline snapshot comparisons (ideally before EOD Fri).
- Put 30 suspicious samples into a shared spreadsheet and tag with quick rubric (Marta + me).
- File a lightweight Jira ticket (CON-3421) linking to this doc and to the spreadsheet.
- If we see confirmed step-up since last release, propose a targeted calibration micro-finetune and a decoding blocklist prototype.

Random heuristics I scribbled:
- If prompt contains words like "original", "first", "who", chance of hallucination increases (intuition).
- Add a noise prompt that asks model to produce 'I don't know' alternatives before final answer; measure acceptance.

Tiny log: 2024-02-10 02:12 PST — initial sweep, flagged 6 high-confidence invents. 2024-02-11 09:35 PST — re-ran temp 0.0 check, reduced to 2.

Footer: informal, messy. Will tidy if this becomes a ticket. For now — rapid triage notes.
